title: Spinal Injuries
body:
Spinal trauma involves damage to the vertebrae, ligaments, or spinal cord, commonly caused by motor
vehicle accidents, falls, or violence.
Symptoms range from pain and numbness to paralysis (tetraplegia/paraplegia) and loss of bodily
functions.
Treatment includes immediate immobilization, surgery, and rehabilitation, with prognosis depending on the
severity and location of the injury.
Practical immobilsation

title: Ribs & Chest
body:
● Causes: Falls, motor vehicle accidents, physical abuse, or severe coughing.
● Symptoms: Intense chest pain, especially with deep breaths, coughing, laughing, or sneezing.
● Signs: Tenderness, swelling, and sometimes audible clicking or crunching (crepitus).
● Pain Control: Regular pain relief (e.g., paracetamol, NSAIDs) is crucial to ensure deep breathing.
● Breathing Exercises: Use an incentive spirometer or take deep breaths often to prevent pneumonia.
● Avoid Smoking: Smoking hinders healing and increases lung infection risk.
● Healing: Rib fractures typically take 6 to 8 weeks, potentially longer in older adults or with osteoporosis.
● Surgery: Severe cases (multiple, displaced fractures or flail chest) may require surgical fixation

title: Untreated, severe rib injuries can lead to:
body:
● Pneumothorax: A collapsed lung.
● Pneumonia: Due to shallow breathing.
● Lung contusion: Bruising of the lung.
● Flail Chest: Multiple ribs broken in multiple places, disrupting the chest wall.

title: Kinematics
body:
Kinematics is the branch of mechanics that describes the
motion of points, objects, and systems without considering the
forces causing them. It focuses on quantifying motion using
position, displacement, velocity, and acceleration, primarily in
one or two dimensions, often applying to projectiles and
moving objects

title: Respiratory Compromise
body:
● A state of impaired breathing, resulting in inadequate oxygen
levels to meet the body’s needs
● Cells have different levels of sensitivity to low oxygen levels:
○ Brain, lung, and heart cells begin to die in 4 to 6 minutes without
oxygen
○ Kidney, liver, and GI tract cells begin to die in 45 to 90 minutes
without oxygen
○ Muscle, bone, and skin cells begin to die in 4 to 6 hours without
oxygen

title: Management: Pitfalls (1 of 2)
body: ● Studies have shown that when assisting a patient to breathe, responders have a tendency to breathe the patient too fast (hyperventilation)

title: Management: Pitfalls (2 of 2)
body:
● Hyperventilation (> 12 breaths/min)
○ Increases pressure in the chest
■ Impairs blood return to the heart, decreases the amount of blood pumped, and decreases blood pressure
○ Reduces carbon dioxide
■ Causes blood vessels to constrict, decreasing oxygen delivery to organs, especially important for the brain

title: Drowning !
body:
Immediate treatment for a drowning casualty focuses on reversing hypoxia (lack of oxygen) by removing them from
water
Open the airway,
Delivering 5 initial rescue breaths followed by CPR (30 chest compressions to 2 breaths).
Call for emergency help immediately.
Treat for hypothermia by removing wet clothing and keeping them warm.
Suctioning
Airway adjunct
Oxygen

title: SHOCK !
body:
Treating shock requires immediate action: call emergency services, lay the person down, raise their legs about 12
inches to improve blood flow, and keep them warm with a blanket. Keep them calm, avoid moving them, and do not
give them anything to drink, even if they are thirsty.
● Call for emergency help: Treat shock as a medical emergency.
● Positioning: Lay the person on their back. If there is no suspected spinal, head, or leg injury, elevate their feet
about 12 inches (30 cm) to assist blood circulation.
● Keep them warm: Cover with a blanket, coat, or whatever is available to prevent heat loss.
● Loosen clothing: Loosen tight clothing around the neck, chest, and waist.
● Manage bleeding: Apply direct pressure to any visible wound.
● Do not feed or hydrate: Do not give food or drink, as it may cause vomiting or choking.
● Recovery Position: If the person is vomiting, bleeding from the mouth, or unconscious but breathing, turn them
onto their side (recovery position) to keep the airway clear, provided there is no spinal injury.
● CPR: If the person is not breathing or showing signs of life, begin CPR immediately
